## Overview
<!-- IMAGE: C++ logo, same float-left treatment as c.qmd's Overview. -->

<!-- What C++ is, and the one-sentence thesis: C++ is not "C with classes plus
extras" but a distinct multi-paradigm language built on the principle of
zero-overhead abstraction. Bjarne Stroustrup, Bell Labs, 1979 ("C with Classes")
→ standardized C++98, then the modern era: C++11, 14, 17, 20, 23. Cross-link
back to the "C is not C++" callout in c.qmd. -->

### A Short History of the Standard
<!-- Timeline table paralleling c.qmd's: C with Classes (1979) → C++98 → C++03
→ C++11 (the "modern C++" inflection: auto, move semantics, lambdas, smart
pointers, range-for) → C++14 → C++17 (structured bindings, optional, variant,
filesystem) → C++20 (concepts, ranges, coroutines, modules) → C++23. Emphasize
that "modern C++" means C++11 and later, and idiomatic modern C++ looks very
different from C++98. -->

### The C++ Philosophy
::: {.subheading}
Zero-overhead abstraction
:::
<!-- The core design tenets: you don't pay for what you don't use; abstractions
should cost no more than the hand-written equivalent; direct hardware access
preserved from C; multi-paradigm (procedural, OO, generic, functional).
Contrast with Rust's safety-first and Python's programmer-time-first stances. -->

## What C++ Adds to C
<!-- Orienting section: the reader knows C. Enumerate at a high level what C++
layers on, each expanded in its own section below. This is the "map." -->

- References (`&`) vs. pointers
- `class` / access control / member functions
- Constructors, destructors, and **RAII**
- Function and operator overloading
- Templates (generic programming)
- The Standard Template Library (STL)
- Exceptions
- Namespaces
- Stronger type safety (`nullptr`, `enum class`, `static_cast` family)

### Small but Pervasive Differences
<!-- The little things that bite a C programmer immediately: bool as a real
keyword, stricter implicit conversions, // comments (well before C99), struct
names as types without typedef, function overloading changing name-mangling,
`nullptr` vs NULL, uniform initialization braces. Quick table. -->

## Types and Declarations
### References
::: {.subheading}
Aliases, not pointers
:::
<!-- `int&` — a reference must bind on declaration, can't be reseated, no null.
Contrast with pointers. Pass-by-reference vs. C's pass-a-pointer idiom.
const references as the idiom for cheap read-only parameters. -->

### `auto` and Type Deduction
<!-- `auto`, `decltype`, when to use them and when they hurt readability. -->

### `enum class`
<!-- Scoped, type-safe enums — the fix for C's leaky enums covered in c.qmd. -->

### Uniform Initialization
<!-- Brace-init `{}`, initializer lists, the most-vexing-parse it solves and the
narrowing it forbids. -->

## Classes and Objects
### From `struct` to `class`
<!-- The only default difference (public vs. private), then everything member
functions add. Anchor to C's "struct + free functions operating on it" pattern. -->

### Member Functions, `this`, and `const` Methods
<!-- Methods, the implicit `this` pointer, const-qualified member functions. -->

### Access Control
<!-- public / private / protected; encapsulation as enforced-by-compiler, unlike
Python's convention-only privacy. -->

### Constructors and Destructors
<!-- Default/parameterized/copy/move constructors, destructor, initializer lists.
Set up RAII, which gets its own section because it's the keystone idea. -->

### RAII
::: {.subheading}
The keystone idea
:::
<!-- Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: tie resource lifetime to object
lifetime; destructor releases. Compare directly to C's manual free/goto-cleanup
ladder (from c.qmd's goto section) and to Rust's ownership/Drop. This is THE
concept that distinguishes C++ from C; give it room. -->

### The Rule of Three / Five / Zero
<!-- If you define one of destructor/copy-ctor/copy-assign you probably need all
three; move semantics make it five; RAII wrapper types let you aim for zero. -->

### Operator Overloading
<!-- Making user types behave like built-ins. Compare to Rust trait impls
(`std::ops`) and Python dunder methods. Cautionary notes on overuse. -->

## Memory Management
### `new` / `delete`
<!-- vs. C's malloc/free; why raw new/delete is now discouraged. -->

### Smart Pointers
<!-- unique_ptr (owning, move-only), shared_ptr (refcounted), weak_ptr. The

<!-- lvalues/rvalues, `std::move`, move constructors; why they exist (avoid deep
